One of the standby powers unlocked by a national emergency. When a declared war or emergency requires use of the armed forces, the Secretary of Defense may build military construction projects that Congress never authorized, using unspent military construction funds.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: 96 Stat. 153](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/96/153){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 10 U.S.C. 2808](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/10/2808?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Trigger: a declaration of war, or a national emergency declared by the President that requires use of the armed forces.
- Projects must be necessary to support that use of the armed forces.
- Funding comes from military construction money already appropriated and not yet obligated.
- Congress must be notified of each decision and its cost.

## Why it matters

Used quietly for overseas projects after 2001, it became prominent in 2019 when 3.6 billion dollars was moved from other projects to border barriers. It is the standard worked example of how the [National Emergencies Act](nea-1976.qmd) converts a proclamation into spending power, and the later cap came through [the annual NDAA](ndaa-annual.qmd).

## Current status

In force. The FY2021 defense authorization capped its use at 500 million dollars per emergency, and 100 million for projects inside the United States.
